atha tṛtīyo vimarśaḥ | (page 70) ekamanuttararūpātprabhṛtitrikaśaktipūritānandam | amṛtāsyamasya jagataḥ pramāṇabhūtaṃ śivaṃ vande || kriyāśaktivijṛmbhā iyamiti abhidhātuṃ sambandhopakramaṃ sāmānyādīnāṃ tattvamupapāditam, adhunātu sambandhatattvameva upapādyate vitatya | tatra paramārthato dvividha eva sambandho jñāpyajñā-pakabhāvo yo jaḍājaḍaniṣṭhaḥ, kāryakāraṇabhāvaśca yo jaḍaniṣṭhaḥ | tatra pūrvo mānameyātmako yanniṣṭhitamuktaṃ vakṣyamāṇaṃ ca siddhyati | pramāṇādhīnā hi vastusiddhayaḥ iti prasiddhametat | ata uktavakṣyamāṇavastusamarthanopayogitayā sambandharūpatayā ca avaśyanirṇetavyaṃ mānameyavyavahāraṃ nirūpayituṃ vimarśāntaraṃ saptadaśabhiḥ sūtraiḥ idametādṛk----------------------------------| ityādibhiḥ ----------īśādivyavahāraḥ pravartyate | ityantaiḥ | ślokadvayena ca atra pramāṇatatphalasvarūpaṃ nirūpyate; tataḥ prameyatattvanirūpaṇāya pratyābhāsaṃ pramāṇavyāpāraḥ, natu niyamena svalakṣaṇātmakavastvekaviśrāntaḥ,-ityamunā tātparyeṇa vimarśabalādābhāsavyavastheti daśakena; tatprasaṅgato mithyājñāna- tattvamekena; prameyatattvaṃ ca prakṛtameva īśvaravāde ghaṭate iti ekena; mānameyaphalavibhāgaḥ sati eva uktarūpe pramātari upapadyate, tata eva na asya prameyatvaṃ yena bhagavatyapi pramāṇaṃ upayujyeta āñjasyena, vyavahāramātrasādhanaṃ tu atra pramāṇamiti trayeṇa,-iti prakaraṇārthaḥ | pratisūtraṃ tu artho nirūpyate | yaduktam- kriyādibuddhayo (page 71) na bhrāntāḥ-iti, tat nirṇetuṃ pramāṇatatphalasvarūpaṃ prasiddhameva anūdyate ślokadvayena idametādṛgityevaṃ yadvaśādvyavatiṣṭhate | vastu pramāṇaṃ tatso'pi svābhāso'bhinavodayaḥ || 1 || so'ntastathāvimarśātmā deśakālādyabhedini | ekābhidhānaviṣaye mitirvastunyabādhitā || 2 || vastu bāhyaṃ nīlādikaṃ, āntaraṃ ca sukhādi yadvaśāt yasya sāmarthyāt vyavatiṣṭhate vibhaktāṃ niyatāṃ maryādāṃ na ativartate idamiti svarūpeṇa, etādṛgiti nityatvādiviśeṣaṇabhūtadharmāntarayogena; tat pramāṇamiti tāvat prasiddhaṃ loke | tatta kiṃ syāditi vivecako
**The valid means: what establishes, and what it produces** Abhinavagupta now turns to the heart of the relation between the known and the knower: the valid means of cognition (pramāṇa). Everything in the world is established through a pramāṇa — nothing is known without one — so before anything else we must determine what a pramāṇa is and what it yields. In the world's ordinary usage, the answer seems simple. The object — the external blue, or the inner pleasure — *by whose force* the cognition stands firm within its own fixed limit, as "this" (by its own form) and "of-this-form" (by some further qualifying feature) — that object is called the valid means. The blue itself, one might say, is what makes the cognition of blue valid. But a moment's reflection undoes this. The object does not stand by its own power alone. If it did, the blue would appear *to me* and not *to Caitra* — it would shine the same for everyone. It appears to me, and so it stands by the power of *another*. And that other cannot be inert: an inert thing could no more establish an appearance than a blind man could guide a blind man. So the other must be of the nature of consciousness. Yet mere consciousness is not enough either. An undifferentiated consciousness could never set blue apart from yellow. What establishes the blue is a consciousness *tinted by* the blue, turned toward the blue, shining *as* the blue — that appearance (ābhāsa) is what sets the blue before us. And the blue it establishes is a *distinct* blue: if the blue were not distinct from consciousness, then the very same consciousness, being one with everything, would have to be yellow too. So the appearance is the shining of a distinct blue — even though, in the deepest sense, the blue is not other than the great light of consciousness, the distinction appears nonetheless. Now comes the grand unification. This whole arising — the contraction of the light by the limiting conditions (the void, the body, the rest) — is *one single act* of the creation-power. And that one act is precisely the illumination of the knower, the means, and the known together (pramātṛ, pramāṇa, prameya). As the siddhapāda puts it: "the one light rises, born of means, object and knower." There is not one power for knowing, another for the means, another for the object; it is all one light, one manifestation. So what, concretely, is the pramāṇa for us, the bound knowers? In the māyā-bound knower — contracted by the body and the rest, turned inward — the appearance, as it were made distinct, faces the external object. As long as it operates, it is tinted by the place and time of the object, changing from moment to moment, a fresh rise each instant. And yet it is one and the same appearance, related to the one knower, spanning endless time. That appearance — my appearance of blue — is the valid means, because it is what does the work of producing the cognition of blue. And what is that cognition — the fruit (pramiti)? It is, Abhinavagupta says, *the very same appearance* turned inward: the awareness (bodhātmā) is the cognition, the fruit of the means. The means and the fruit are not two separate things, nor are they mere synonyms. The means is the appearance facing outward, of the nature of light; the fruit is the same appearance facing inward, of the nature of reflexive-awareness, contracted by the tint of the object, taking the form of the word. In a single thing the cause and its fruit are both discerned — as in the blue-light and its reflexive-awareness. And the proof that the fruit is the reflexive-awareness is that the operation is the fruit (for the instrument's first achievement is its operation), and the operation is non-different from the agent being operated. So, in the primary sense, the means and the fruit are one; whatever *further* fruit there is — the purpose served, the activity, the attainment — may be something else again. > The passage asks what really makes a cognition valid. Ordinary discourse appears to locate the > validating force in the object itself: a cognition of blue is stable because the blue object > determines it. Abhinavagupta argues that this cannot be sufficient. If the object possessed this > determining force simply in itself, its appearance would not be restricted to one subject rather than > another. Its manifestation therefore depends upon consciousness. He then pushes the argument further: > knower, means of knowledge, and known object are not ultimately three independently functioning > factors, but aspects of a single manifestation or "light." The point of the passage is thus to > relocate the operation of *pramāṇa* from an independently existing object to the event of > manifestation itself. > > The exact account of how this single manifestation becomes restricted to particular knowers is > developed in the following discussion.
